opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the more troubling trends we've seen, and honestly it's a little insidious because on the surface it can look like progress. You open a magazine or a brand's campaign and you see more diversity in the faces, and you think, great, the industry is finally listening. But then you find out those models don't exist. They were generated.

And what that really does is it takes the appearance of representation and strips out the substance of it. The whole point of representation was never just about pixels on a page showing a certain skin tone. It's about actual people from those communities getting the jobs, getting paid, building careers, getting their names out there, having a seat in that industry. Modeling, photography, styling, makeup, all of those are real livelihoods. When you swap in a synthetic person, you get to claim the diversity credit without hiring anyone from the community you say you're representing. It's kind of the worst of both worlds.

There's also the question of where those generated images come from. These models are trained on enormous amounts of scraped imagery, including photographs of real people, real models, real artists' work, almost always without consent and without compensation. So in a sense you're taking from the very communities that have historically been underrepresented, and then using that to produce a product that replaces them. That's a pretty bitter irony.

And then there's the authenticity piece. A generated face is essentially an average, a statistical blend of what the model has seen. It can reinforce stereotypes rather than challenge them, because it's reproducing whatever patterns dominate the training data. Real people bring individuality, lived experience, a perspective. A generated image is someone else's idea of what a person of color should look like.

So I'd say, I understand the economic pressures that push companies toward this, it's cheaper, it's faster, there are no contracts to negotiate. But I think audiences, and the industry, should see it for what it is. It's not representation. It's a simulation of representation, and it actively undercuts the people who fought to make real representation happen in the first place.

r001.rationale: The candidate says companies face economic pressure and that using generated models is “cheaper,” identifying lower cost as a reason for the replacement.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this one really gets to me, honestly. So the case that got a lot of attention was Levi's, and then there were a few magazines and fashion outlets that essentially said, "We want more diversity in our imagery, so we're going to generate AI models of color instead of hiring them." And I think if you step back, it's almost a perfect illustration of what's wrong with how these tools are being deployed.

Think about what's actually happening there. You have an entire group of people who have historically been underrepresented in these industries, who have fought for decades to get a seat at the table, to get the bookings, to be visible. And now the moment the industry decides representation matters, the response isn't "let's hire more of these folks," it's "let's synthesize their likeness so we can get the optics without paying anyone." You get the appearance of inclusion, but the actual humans who would benefit from that inclusion are cut out entirely. It's representation as a costume.

And the thing is, those generated images don't come from nowhere. These models are trained on photos of real people, real models, real photographers' work, almost always without consent and without compensation. So in a sense you're taking from exactly the community you claim to be elevating, and then using the output to replace them. That's a double hit.

The other piece that I think people underestimate is the labor dynamics. Fashion and editorial work is already precarious. If you're a working model of color, you're competing for a smaller pool of jobs to begin with. If brands can just prompt their way to a "diverse" campaign, those jobs evaporate, and they evaporate first for the people with the least leverage. So it's not just symbolic harm, it's economic.

I'll say, I don't think most of the people making these decisions are cartoon villains. It's usually framed as efficiency, or as a supplement, "we'll do both." But in practice, once the cheap option exists, it tends to become the default. We've seen that pattern over and over.

So from my perspective, coming from the work we've been doing on protecting artists from unauthorized training, this is the same story in a different domain. The technology isn't the problem per se, it's that it's being pointed at the people with the least power and the least ability to say no. If magazines genuinely care about representation, the answer is pretty simple, and it's not a diffusion model. It's hiring people.

r001.rationale: The response says magazines can synthesize models to get inclusion optics “without paying anyone” and describes the generated option as cheap, identifying lower cost as a reason for replacement.

astra-6.text:
I think that confuses the appearance of diversity with actual representation. You can generate an image of a person of color, but who got hired? Who got paid? Who had a voice in how they were portrayed? If none of those opportunities went to people from that community, then you haven’t really addressed the underlying problem.

And that’s what troubles me about using AI this way. There’s an opportunity to expand participation, but instead you’re using it to create the impression of participation while leaving the people themselves out. For me, representation has to involve more than the pixels on the page.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes AI-generated models for creating the appearance of diversity while excluding people from the community, but it does not identify lower cost as a reason magazines use them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to ask what representation is supposed to accomplish. If it’s simply having a face with a particular skin tone on a page, then sure, you can generate that. But that’s a very shallow definition of representation. You haven’t hired a model of color. You haven’t given someone an opportunity, compensated them, or brought their perspective into the process.

What bothers me is the idea that you can take a lack of diversity and solve it by changing the pixels, while leaving the people and the decisions behind those images exactly the same. You get the appearance of inclusion without doing the work of inclusion. And if those generated images replace opportunities for real people who already struggle to get access to that industry, then you may actually be making the underlying problem worse.

r001.rationale: The response discusses superficial representation and lost opportunities for real models, but does not identify lower cost as a reason magazines use AI-generated models.
